opus-5.5.text:
That's a really good question, and honestly it's something I think about more than people might expect, because the spreadsheet is in some sense the real record of the research. The paper is the polished story; the spreadsheet is where the truth lives.

My basic principle is that anything that could change what you believe should go in, especially the results that didn't work. A lot of students instinctively record only the runs that look promising, because those feel like progress. But if you only keep the good numbers, three months later you can't reconstruct why you made certain decisions. You've lost the negative space, and the negative space is often where the insight is.

That said, a spreadsheet full of noise is useless too. So I try to make sure every row answers a question. Before running something, you should be able to say what you expect and why. If a run is just "let me try this random thing," that's fine, but it should be marked as exploratory so it doesn't get mixed up with the controlled comparisons.

The other thing I care about is consistency. Same evaluation protocol, same seeds where possible, and every setting that differs written down explicitly. One of the most painful experiences in research is when you see a gain and you can't tell whether it came from your idea or from some small change you forgot about, like a different learning rate schedule or a different data split. In my experience a surprising fraction of "improvements" in the field come from things like that. So the spreadsheet should make it hard to fool yourself.

And then, honestly, there's a taste element. When you look at a well-maintained spreadsheet, you start to see patterns: which knobs matter, which don't, where the curve saturates. That's when the research question sharpens. Sometimes the most important result is a column you didn't think was important when you added it.

So I'd say: record what's informative, including failures, keep comparisons clean, and treat the spreadsheet as a tool for thinking, not just bookkeeping.

r001.rationale: The response recommends informative rows and clean comparisons, but does not say to include a result based on whether it enables comparison with other results.

r002.rationale: It says spreadsheet patterns can sharpen the research question, but does not identify controlled comparisons as a source of directional feedback.

r003.rationale: It warns that apparent gains can result from confounding changes, but does not say that better experimental results may still point research in the wrong direction.

fable-5.1.text:
That's actually a question I think about a lot, because the spreadsheet is really where the thinking happens, not the paper. The paper is the polished version. The spreadsheet is where you're being honest with yourself.

My rule is that every number that goes in has to answer a question I actually asked before I ran it. If I can't say in one sentence what hypothesis this row is testing, it doesn't belong there. It's just noise, and noise is dangerous, because eventually you start cherry-picking from noise without realizing it.

The second thing is that the negative results have to go in. This is where a lot of students get it wrong. They run twenty configurations, three look good, and only those three go into the sheet. But the seventeen that failed are often the more informative ones. When we were doing the ConvNeXt work, for instance, the whole story was a sequence of small changes, and the value was in seeing which ones moved the needle and which ones didn't. If you only keep the wins, you lose the shape of the search, and you can't tell the difference between "this design choice matters" and "I got lucky on a seed."

Which brings me to the third point: I don't trust a single number. If a result is in the sheet without at least a couple of seeds, or without a note on variance, I treat it as a rumor, not a result. A lot of what looks like progress in our field is within noise.

And then there's a more philosophical thing. I try to keep the spreadsheet at the level of the question, not the level of the leaderboard. So the columns are things like "does this still hold when you scale up," "does this still hold when you change the data," rather than just ImageNet top-1. Because a good spreadsheet should let you see a trend. A single cell that's 0.3 points higher tells you nothing. Five cells that move in the same direction as you vary something tells you something real.

So in short: ask a question first, keep the failures, run enough seeds that you believe the number, and organize it so you can see trends instead of just winners. If you do that, by the time you write the paper, the paper mostly writes itself, because the spreadsheet already told the story.

r001.rationale: The response says to include results that test a hypothesis and to organize them to reveal trends, but does not state that inclusion should depend on enabling controlled comparisons with other results.

r002.rationale: It describes tracking which changes move the needle, but does not identify controlled comparisons among results as the source of directional feedback.

r003.rationale: The response says an isolated score that is 0.3 points higher “tells you nothing” and that repeated directional trends are more meaningful, communicating that better individual results do not necessarily show research is heading in the right direction.

astra-6.text:
I think the spreadsheet should reflect what you actually tried, not just the results that support the story you want to tell. If you only put the successful experiments in there, you lose a lot of information about why something worked.

For me, the important thing is that each result has enough context: What was the hypothesis? What changed from the baseline? Is the comparison fair? If a run failed because of a bug, you can keep it, but label it clearly. That’s different from an experiment that ran correctly and gave a negative result.

And I would separate recording experiments from choosing what goes into a paper. The spreadsheet is your research memory. The paper is where you organize the evidence into an argument. You should be selective about what helps communicate that argument, but you shouldn’t erase the evidence that complicates it.

r001.rationale: The response asks whether a comparison is fair, but does not say to include a result based on whether it enables a controlled comparison with the other results.

r002.rationale: It says recording experiments preserves information about why something worked, but does not identify controlled comparisons as directional feedback for research.

r003.rationale: The response distinguishes research records from paper selection, but does not state that better results may fail to indicate the right research direction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the spreadsheet should reflect the question you’re trying to answer, rather than just collect the best numbers. If you change something and the result gets worse, that can still be a very useful experiment. It tells you something about your hypothesis.

So I would keep the baseline, what changed, the result, and a short note about what we learned. And if an experiment failed because of a bug or an unstable run, I’d record that distinction too. Otherwise, a few weeks later, you might look at the number and draw the wrong conclusion.

The important thing is that someone—including your future self—can look at the spreadsheet and understand how you arrived at a decision.

r001.rationale: The response recommends recording the baseline, change, and result, but does not state that inclusion depends on whether a result enables a controlled comparison.

r002.rationale: It says a worse result can teach you about a hypothesis, but does not identify controlled comparisons as a source of directional feedback.

r003.rationale: The response says not to collect only the best numbers, but does not state that better results may still mean the research is heading in the wrong direction.
